title: Indian Painting
summary: Painting began in the pre-historic rock paintings of Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh), with animals; cave paintings at Narsinghgarh show drying skins of spotted deer; paintings also appeared on Harappan seals. Literature mentions three types: lepyacitras (representation of folklore), lekhacitras (line drawing and painting on textile) and dhulicitras (painting on the floor). The Vinayapitaka (4th–3rd century BC) mentions painted figures in royal buildings; Mudrarakshasa (5th century AD) mentions patas; Vatsyayana's Kamasutra counts painting among 64 arts; the Vishnudharmottara Purana (7th century) has the Chitrasutra on the six limbs of painting. The best Gupta paintings are at Ajanta (animals, birds, trees, flowers, human figures and Jataka stories): murals in cave 9 show monks going to a stupa and cave 10 Jataka stories; the best are of the 5th–6th centuries, mostly religious but with secular scenes of princes, ladies, coolies, beggars, peasants and ascetics. Colours used: red ochre, kum kum or sindura red, yellow ochre (haritala), indigo, lapis lazuli blue (from outside India), lampblack, chalk white, terra verte and green. Other Buddhist and classical sites: Bagh, Badami cave 3, Kanchipuram, Sittanavasal (Jain, 'abode of the Jaina Siddhas'), Ellora (Kailasa and Jain caves), Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjavur, Malayadipatti and Tirunalaipuram.

In the Delhi Sultanate murals showed flowers, leaves and plants in palaces and mosques; Persian and Arabic influence and illustrated manuscripts arrived; the Gwalior palace paintings of Man Singh Tomar impressed Babur and Akbar. In the 14th–15th centuries miniature painting emerged in Gujarat and Rajasthan under rich Jain merchants (manuscripts of the Tirthankaras' lives), with Mandu, Jaunpur and Bengal as centres; under the Palas (9th–10th century) palm-leaf miniatures resembled Ajanta on a small scale. Under the Mughals book illumination and individual miniatures replaced wall painting. Humayun brought two Persian painters; Akbar patronised artists from Kashmir and Gujarat; painters' names were recorded for the first time; great painters: Abd-us-Samad, Dasawanth, Basawan; illustrations in the Baburnama and Akbarnama; the synthesis of Persian and Indian styles produced an independent Mughal style; about 1400 cloth paintings (1562–77); portraits encouraged. Painting reached its climax under Jahangir, himself a painter and connoisseur: vibrant peacock blue and red, three-dimensional effect; Mansur (birds and animals; portrait of Abul Hasan), Bishan Das and Manohar. Shah Jahan preferred architecture, but Dara Shikoh patronised painting (plants and animals). Aurangzeb's withdrawal of royal patronage dispersed artists, helping the Rajasthani and Pahari schools, whose miniatures drew themes from epics, myths, Barahmasa (seasons) and Ragamala (melodies); local centres: Kangra, Kulu, Basoli, Guler, Chamba, Garhwal, Bilaspur and Jammu. Bhakti inspired illustrated Vaishnava texts.

In the late 18th and early 19th century semi-westernised local styles (Company style) were patronised by the British: Shaikh Zia-ud-Din's bird studies for Lady Impey and Ghulam Ali Khan's portraits for William Fraser and Colonel Skinner. Later art schools on the European model opened in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras; Raja Ravi Varma's oil paintings of mythological and social themes became very popular. The Bengal School (Rabindranath and Abanindranath Tagore, E.B. Havell, Ananda Coomaraswamy) flowered at Santiniketan where Tagore set up Kala Bhavan; Nandalal Bose (folk and Japanese art), Binod Behari Mukherjee (oriental traditions), Ramkinkar Baij; Jamini Roy drew on Orissa pata and Kalighat painting; Amrita Shergil studied in Paris and Budapest and painted Indian women and peasants in bright colours. In 1943 the Calcutta Group (Paritosh Sen, Nirode Mazumdar, Pradosh Dasgupta) depicted the condition of the people; the Progressive Artists Group was formed in Bombay in 1948 under F.N. Souza with S.H. Raza, M.F. Hussain, K.H. Ara, S.K. Bakre and H.A. Gade, breaking away from the Bengal School; in the 1970s artists took up poverty, corruption and communal tension; the Madras School under D.P. Roy Chowdhury and K.C.S. Paniker became important. Other modern artists: Tyeb Mehta, Satish Gujral, Krishen Khanna, Manjit Bawa, K.G. Subramanyan, Anjolie Ela Menon, Akbar Padamsee, Jatin Das, Jehangir Sabavala and A. Ramachandran. The National Gallery of Modern Art has the largest collection of modern art and the Lalit Kala Akademi patronises artists.

Rangoli (North), alpana (Bengal), aipan (Uttarakhand), rangavalli (Karnataka), kolam (Tamil Nadu) and mandana (Madhya Pradesh) are floor designs, usually of rice powder, coloured powder or petals. Mithila (Madhubani) painting of Bihar is made by village women with vegetable colours and a few earth colours, finished in black lines on cow-dung-treated paper; subjects: Sita's exile, Ram–Lakshman in the forest, Lakshmi, Ganesha, Hanuman, sun, moon, tulsi, court scenes and weddings; drawings are conceptual; mothers make them in advance as marriage gifts conveying advice on married life; upper classes use colours, lower castes red and black line work; the technique passes from mother to daughter. Kalamkari (done by kalam, pen) in Andhra Pradesh: hand painting and block printing with vegetable dyes on cloth; Sri Kalahasti and Machilipatnam; temple cloth panels developed under Vijayanagara patronage in the 15th century; subjects from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and mythology scene after scene with floral borders; outlines by hand-carved blocks and finer details by the pen made of bamboo or date palm; Masulipatnam style has Persian motifs from Golconda; dyes from roots, leaves and salts of iron, tin, copper and alum. Orissa Patachitra: detailed painting on cloth similar to Kalighat pats. Phad: scroll painting of Rajasthan (Bhilwara, Shahpura), 700 years old, depicting local deities and heroes, narrated by singers; bold lines and flat two-dimensional figures arranged in sections. Gond art: figurative works of the Gond tribe. Batik: imported from the Orient and now Indianised. Warli painting: named after a small tribe of Maharashtra, painted by women on floors and walls of homes and places of worship in white rice paste on a plain background using geometric shapes (squares, triangles, circles), dots and crooked lines, spiralling composition; secular and not religious iconography. Kalighat painting: from Kalighat in Kolkata, early 19th century, by Patua painters on paper in water colours with sweeping lines, bright colours and a clear background; Kali, Lakshmi, Krishna, Ganesha, Shiva and also social comment on babus, courtesans and actresses; inspired by photography, western theatre and babu culture; considered the first works of art from Bengal. Handicrafts: Kashmir shawls, carpets, namdar silk, walnut furniture; Rajasthan bandhani, jewellery, minakari, blue pottery; Andhra Bidri and Pochampalli saris; Tamil Nadu bronze and Kanjeevaram silk; Mysore silk and sandalwood; Kerala ivory and rosewood; Chanderi and Kosa silk of MP; Lucknow chikan; Banaras brocade; Assam cane; Bankura terracotta.

vsa: How are paintings helpful in knowing about the past?
Paintings show the life, customs, dress, buildings and beliefs of people of those times, how kings and courtiers dressed and sat in assembly, and so they are valuable historical records.
Write any two brief characteristic features of Patachitras.
They are mostly painted on cloth and are highly detailed, similar to the Kalighat pats; they depict religious and mythological themes.
Describe any two features of Kalighat painting.

It was painted on paper in water colours with clear sweeping lines, bright colours and a plain background; subjects were gods and goddesses and later social life of Bengal such as babus and courtesans.
Mention two materials used for making Mithila paintings.
Vegetable colours with a few earth colours and cow-dung treated paper, finished with black lines.
What is meant by miniature painting?
Small paintings on a small surface, on perishable materials like palm leaves or paper, illustrating manuscripts and themes from epics, myths, seasons (Barahmasa) and melodies (Ragamala).
Name two features of Warli painting.
White rice paste on a plain background using geometric shapes and dots and crooked lines in spiralling compositions, painted by women, secular in character.
Name two institutions set up to promote art in India.
The National Gallery of Modern Art and the Lalit Kala Akademi.
sa: Write an account of Batik paint.

Batik is a wax-resist dyeing and painting technique imported from the Orient and now Indianised into a mature and expensive art: wax is applied to parts of the cloth so they do not take dye, producing designs after dyeing and removing the wax.
Describe three distinctive features of Kalamkari art.

It is hand painting and block printing on cloth with vegetable dyes from roots, leaves and mineral salts; subjects from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and mythology painted scene after scene with floral borders; outlines by hand-carved blocks and details with a pen of bamboo or date palm; Sri Kalahasti and Machilipatnam are centres.

Named after the Warli tribe of Maharashtra, it is painted by women on floors and walls using white rice paste on a plain contrasting background in geometric patterns of squares, triangles and circles with dots and crooked lines; trees, birds and daily life are shown in a spiralling composition; it is more secular than other tribal arts.

It is the folk art of the Mithila region of Bihar, made by village women with vegetable and earth colours and black lines on cow-dung treated paper; it shows Sita's exile, gods, sun, moon, tulsi, weddings and court scenes; it is conceptual, made for rituals, and mothers make pieces as gifts for daughters, conveying advice on married life.
Write about the Progressive Artists Group.

Formed in Bombay in 1948 (1947 in the textbook for Lesson 9) under F.N. Souza with S.H. Raza, M.F. Hussain, K.H. Ara, S.K. Bakre and H.A. Gade, it broke away from the Bengal School and represented the modern forceful art of independent India.
la: Describe the development of the art of painting during the medieval period.

Under the Delhi Sultanate murals of flowers and plants decorated palaces and mosques and Persian influence came with illustrated manuscripts. Jain merchants patronised miniature manuscripts in Gujarat and Rajasthan (14th–15th centuries) and the Palas produced palm-leaf miniatures in the east. The Mughals replaced wall painting with book illumination: Humayun brought Persian painters; Akbar encouraged portraits, cloth paintings and illustrations (Baburnama, Akbarnama) and a Persian–Indian synthesis; under Jahangir painting reached its climax with vibrant colours and depth (Mansur, Bishan Das, Manohar). Aurangzeb withdrew patronage, dispersing artists who developed Rajasthani and Pahari schools with themes from epics, Barahmasa and Ragamala.
Explain the contribution of the Mughals to painting.

The Mughals began a new era by synthesising Indian painting with the Persian tradition. Humayun brought Persian painters; Akbar patronised Hindu and Persian artists, recorded their names and produced illustrated manuscripts and portraits; Jahangir, himself a connoisseur, took the art to its zenith with vibrant colours and a three-dimensional effect, while Mansur painted birds and animals; Dara Shikoh patronised painting; Mughal court painters introduced landscapes with human figures and signed miniatures.
Describe the emergence of the Bengal School and the Progressive Artists Group.

After British-style art schools and Ravi Varma's oil painting, the Bengal School grew under Abanindranath and Rabindranath Tagore, E.B. Havell and Ananda Coomaraswamy at Santiniketan's Kala Bhavan, with Nandalal Bose, Binod Behari Mukherjee and Ramkinkar Baij reviving Indian themes. In 1943 the Calcutta Group depicted the people's condition. In 1948 the Progressive Artists Group of Bombay (Souza, Raza, Hussain, Ara, Bakre, Gade) broke away from the Bengal School to express the modern art of independent India; the Madras School under Roy Chowdhury and Paniker followed.
Discuss the significance of painting as a part of culture.

Painting expresses the basic human need for expression from prehistoric rock art to modern art; it records the life, dress and beliefs of each age (Ajanta, Mughal miniatures, Kalighat), mixes religious and secular themes, shows the synthesis of traditions (Persian and Indian), carries folk traditions from mother to daughter (Mithila, Warli) and reflects social change and nationalism in the modern period.
